title: The critical signal fraction for local entropy concavity
shortTitle: How much noise restores entropy concavity? Exactly enough to push the signal below 4/7
oneLine: Mix two noisy copies of a near-Gaussian symmetric signal: the entropy of the blend is guaranteed concave in the mixing weight exactly when the noise variance exceeds three quarters of the signal variance (signal fraction below 4/7, signal-to-noise ratio 4/3); whether 4/7 itself qualifies is open.
abstract: Take two independent copies of a random signal, add Gaussian noise to each, and mix the noisy copies with weights √t and √(1−t). Ball, Nayar and Tkocz conjectured that, for log-concave signals, the entropy of the mixture is concave in t. Luo (2026) disproved this and showed that symmetric near-Gaussian counterexamples survive added noise whenever the signal accounts for more than 4/7 of the total variance; Schubr (2026) proved local concavity below 1/2. This candidate shows that 4/7 is the true local threshold for symmetric signals. For every signal fraction q < 4/7 there is an explicit neighbourhood of the Gaussian, defined by a uniform bound on the relative density f/φ − 1, in which every symmetric variance-one input gives a strictly concave entropy curve (Theorem A); with Luo's counterexamples, 4/7 is the supremum of such signal fractions, a signal-to-noise ratio of 4/3. Whether q = 4/7 itself qualifies is open. For every q in (4/7, 1], one sequence of smooth strongly log-concave inputs makes equal weighting a strict local entropy minimum, with exact curvature constant γ(q) = 21√5 q/(49q − 4) and a Gaussian-shaped local profile (Theorem B); the sign on (4/7, 2 − √2], Luo's Problem 10.3, was also proposed in an earlier public, unrefereed GitHub argument. The threshold is the fixed point q = b(q/2) of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck smoothing inequality whose range is proved sharp, with Luo's family extremal within the Hermite test functions (Proposition S); at q = 4/7 Luo's family is strictly concave near equal weighting (Proposition E); the proof's radius shrinks like (4/7 − Q)^(9/4) (Remark R). The effects are minute (dips of order 10⁻¹³ nats); the results are structural. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem A (proof): for every Q < 4/7 there is an explicit δ_Q > 0 such that every admissible even g with ‖g‖∞ ≤ δ_Q gives F'' ≤ −(1/16)‖N(T_√(qt) g + T_√(q(1−t)) g)‖² < 0 for all q ≤ Q and t in [0, 1]; δ_0.5 ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵.
Corollary (proof, with Luo 2026): (0, 4/7) ⊆ C ⊆ (0, 4/7], so sup C = 4/7, a noise variance of 3/4 of the signal variance (signal-to-noise ratio 4/3); whether 4/7 ∈ C is open.

Theorem B (proof): for every q in (4/7, 1], one sequence of smooth strongly log-concave inputs gives F''(1/2) > 0 eventually, with γ(q) = 21√5 q/(49q − 4) and local profile 1 − exp(−4γ(q)s²); the sign on (4/7, 2 − √2] was also proposed in an earlier public GitHub argument.

Proposition S (proof): the bounded-input smoothing inequality ‖T_√s g‖² ≤ J‖g‖∞‖T_√r g‖ holds for s < b(r) = √(2r(1+r)) − r and fails beyond; 4/7 is the fixed point q = b(q/2), and Luo's parameter a = 7/(3√5) is extremal within the Hermite test functions.

Proposition E and Remark R (proof): at q = 4/7 Luo's family is strictly concave near t = 1/2, so it gives no boundary counterexample; the proof's radius decays like C_δ(4/7 − Q)^(9/4), C_δ ≈ 5.93 × 10⁻³.

narration: How much noise does it take to make entropy behave? An Evidence Press briefing. Take two independent copies of a random signal, add Gaussian noise to each, and blend the two noisy copies, with a mixing weight that runs from all of one copy to an even blend. Mixing tends to make things more Gaussian, and Gaussians have the most entropy, so a natural guess is that entropy rises smoothly as you blend, with no dips: in mathematical terms, that it is a concave function of the mixing weight. Ball, Nayar and Tkocz conjectured exactly this. This year Luo disproved it, and showed that tiny symmetric bumps on a Gaussian signal can still create a dip at an even blend whenever the signal makes up more than four sevenths of the total variance. Below one half, a positive result was already known. The question was what happens in between. This paper answers it. For any signal fraction below four sevenths, every symmetric signal close enough to a Gaussian gives a concave entropy curve. In noise terms: concavity is guaranteed once the noise variance exceeds three quarters of the signal variance, a signal-to-noise ratio of four thirds. Above that level the paper sharpens the counterexamples, with an exact formula for the dip's curvature. Part of that sign was proposed shortly before, in a public online argument, which the paper cites. It also explains where four sevenths comes from: the fixed point of a sharp Gaussian smoothing inequality. Two cautions. These are local results, and the effects are minute, dips of around ten to the minus thirteen in entropy. And whether exactly four sevenths itself qualifies is still open. The proofs are written out, and checked by standard-library scripts that must catch sixteen deliberately broken copies. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, published on the third of November twenty twenty-six; its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Treat 4/7 as the exact supremum of signal fractions at which Gaussian noise restores local mixing-weight entropy concavity for symmetric near-Gaussian inputs in uniform relative-density neighbourhoods; treat q = 4/7 itself as open.
decisionObject.scope: Two independent identical even variance-one inputs, mixing weights √t and √(1−t), Gaussian noise, inputs within a uniform relative-density neighbourhood of the Gaussian. Global (non-local) concavity, asymmetric inputs and the boundary are not settled.
